stem: A team uses GitHub Flow. Which rule is central to that model?

options.text: `main` is always deployable; work happens on short branches merged by pull request
options.why: GitHub Flow has one long-lived branch that stays releasable, plus short feature branches reviewed in PRs.

options.text: Features merge into a long-lived `develop` branch before a release branch is cut
options.why: That describes GitFlow, which adds develop, release and hotfix branches.

options.text: Everyone commits directly to `main` and reviews happen after deployment
options.why: GitHub Flow routes every change through a pull request before it reaches main.

options.text: Each release gets its own permanent branch that is never merged back into the main line
options.why: Permanent release branches are a release-maintenance pattern, not GitHub Flow.

explanation: GitHub Flow is deliberately simple: branch from main, commit, open a pull request, review and test, merge, deploy. Because main must always be deployable, the PR is the gate where review and CI happen.

stem: A draft pull request cannot be merged until it is marked as ready for review.

options.text: True
options.why: Draft PRs signal work in progress; the merge button stays disabled until the PR is marked ready.

options.text: False
options.why: GitHub blocks merging drafts, so authors can share early work without risking an accidental merge.

explanation: Drafts let you open a PR early for visibility or CI feedback. They cannot be merged, and code owners are not automatically requested to review them until the PR is marked ready for review.
reference: GitHub docs: About pull requests (draft pull requests)

stem: A pull request into the default branch fixes issue #12. What should its description contain so the issue closes automatically when the PR is merged?

options.text: `Related to #12`
options.why: A plain reference links the issue in the timeline, but "related to" is not a closing keyword.

options.text: `Fixes #12`
options.why: "Fixes" is one of the closing keywords, so merging into the default branch closes #12.

options.text: `See issue 12 for details`
options.why: Without the `#` reference and a closing keyword, GitHub creates no link and closes nothing.

options.text: `@12 resolved`
options.why: The `@` sign mentions users and teams, not issues, so this neither links nor closes anything.

explanation: Closing keywords are close/closes/closed, fix/fixes/fixed and resolve/resolves/resolved, followed by an issue reference. They take effect when the PR is merged into the repository's default branch.
reference: GitHub docs: Linking a pull request to an issue

stem: In Conventional Commits, which type prefix marks a commit that adds a new feature (for example `____: add CSV export`)? Type just the type.
explanation: `feat` introduces a new feature and maps to a MINOR version bump; `fix` patches a bug and maps to PATCH. Other types such as `docs`, `chore` or `refactor` are allowed but don't imply a release on their own.

stem: Which commit subject line follows the widely used Git convention?

options.text: `Fixed the bug where the login button didn't work on Safari and also tidied some CSS.`
options.why: It is past tense, far over 50 characters, mixes two changes and ends with a period.

options.text: `Fix login button click handling in Safari`
options.why: Imperative mood, under about 50 characters, no trailing period, one change.

options.text: `fixes`
options.why: It says nothing about what changed, which makes history and blame useless.

options.text: `WIP - more changes to login stuff (see PR)`
options.why: WIP subjects describe the process, not the change, and age badly once merged.

explanation: A good subject reads like a command ("Fix…", "Add…"), completing "If applied, this commit will…". Keep it to about 50 characters, leave a blank line, then explain the why in a body wrapped at about 72 characters.

stem: Match each repository role in a GitHub organization with what it is meant for.

options.text: Read
options.why: Can view and clone the repository, open issues and comment.

options.text: Triage
options.why: Can manage issues and pull requests without write access to code.

options.text: Write
options.why: Can push to the repository and merge pull requests.

options.text: Admin
options.why: Full control, including managing access and dangerous settings.

prompts.text: A community member who should only view, clone and discuss
A support lead who labels, assigns and closes issues but never pushes code
A developer who pushes branches and merges pull requests
The person who manages collaborator access and repository settings

explanation: From least to most access the roles are Read, Triage, Write, Maintain and Admin. Triage exists precisely so people can manage issues and PRs without code write access; Maintain manages the repository without sensitive or destructive actions; only Admin manages access.
reference: GitHub docs: Repository roles for an organization

stem: In an issue comment you write `@acme/frontend please take a look`. What happens?

options.text: Only the team's maintainers are notified, and only if they watch the repository
options.why: A team mention notifies the team's members, not just its maintainers.

options.text: Members of the `frontend` team in the `acme` organization are notified
options.why: Team mentions use `@org/team-name` and notify everyone on that team.

options.text: GitHub assigns the issue to every member of the team automatically
options.why: Mentions notify people; assignment is a separate action.

options.text: Nothing happens because teams can only be mentioned in pull requests
options.why: Team mentions work in issues, pull requests and discussions alike.

explanation: Mentioning `@username` notifies one person; `@org/team` notifies the members of that team (the team must be visible to you). It is a lightweight way to pull the right people into a conversation without assigning them.
reference: GitHub docs: Basic writing and formatting syntax (Mentioning people and teams)

stem: Which Markdown renders as an unchecked task-list item in a GitHub issue?

options.text: `- [ ] Write migration`
options.why: A list marker, a space, then `[ ]` creates a checkbox; `[x]` checks it.

options.text: `[ ] - Write migration`
options.why: The list marker has to come first; this renders as plain text.

options.text: `* (todo) Write migration`
options.why: Parentheses have no special meaning; this is an ordinary bullet.

options.text: `- [-] Write migration`
options.why: Only a space or `x` inside the brackets makes a task; `-` renders literally.

explanation: Task lists use `- [ ]` and `- [x]`. In issues they show progress and can be ticked from the UI, which makes them handy for checklists in PR templates and planning issues.

stem: A team wants `main` to have a linear history with exactly one commit per merged pull request. Which merge method fits?

options.text: Create a merge commit
options.why: This keeps every PR commit and adds a merge commit, so history is not linear.

options.text: Squash and merge
options.why: All PR commits are combined into one new commit on main, with no merge commit.

options.text: Rebase and merge
options.why: History is linear, but every commit from the PR lands individually on main.

options.text: Merge locally with `--no-ff` and push
options.why: A no-fast-forward merge always records a merge commit.

explanation: Squash and merge produces one commit per PR and keeps history linear. Rebase and merge also avoids merge commits but replays each commit. A merge commit preserves the branch's commits plus a merge commit with two parents.
reference: GitHub docs: About merge methods on GitHub

stem:
A CODEOWNERS file contains these lines, in this order:

```
*        @acme/platform
*.js     @alice
/docs/   @acme/writers
```

A PR changes only `docs/setup.js`. Who is automatically requested for review?

options.text: `@acme/platform`, `@alice` and `@acme/writers` together
options.why: Owners don't accumulate: only the last matching pattern decides.

options.text: `@alice`, because the `*.js` rule is more specific
options.why: CODEOWNERS uses order, not specificity; a later match overrides `*.js`.

options.text: `@acme/writers`
options.why: The last matching pattern takes precedence, and `/docs/` matches this file last.

options.text: `@acme/platform`, because `*` comes first
options.why: The first line is only a fallback; later matching lines override it.

explanation: CODEOWNERS is read top to bottom and the last pattern that matches a path wins. Put broad defaults first and specific overrides later. Code owners must also have write access for the request to happen.

stem: Where can a single pull request template live so GitHub uses it to prefill new pull requests?

options.text: Only `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/pull_request.yml`
options.why: That folder is for issue templates and forms, not pull request templates.

options.text: `pull_request_template.md` in the root, `docs/` or `.github/`
options.why: GitHub looks for that file name in any of the three supported locations.

options.text: A `PR.md` file placed anywhere in the repository, which GitHub discovers automatically
options.why: GitHub only recognises the documented file name and locations.

options.text: In the repository settings, under the Pull requests section
options.why: Templates are files in the repository, not settings.

explanation: Name the file `pull_request_template.md` and put it in the repository root, `docs/` or `.github/`. For several templates, use a `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/` subdirectory and choose one with the `template` query parameter.
reference: GitHub docs: Creating a pull request template for your repository

stem: A project uses Conventional Commits with semantic-release defaults. Which commits trigger a new release? (Choose two.)

options.text: `fix(api): handle empty payloads`
options.why: `fix` maps to a PATCH release.

options.text: `feat(ui): add dark mode toggle`
options.why: `feat` maps to a MINOR release.

options.text: `docs: clarify setup steps`
options.why: Documentation commits don't trigger a release by default.

options.text: `chore: bump dev dependencies`
options.why: Chores are bookkeeping and don't release on their own.

options.text: `style: reformat with prettier`
options.why: Formatting-only changes don't imply a release.

explanation: Conventional Commits ties types to SemVer: `fix` → PATCH, `feat` → MINOR, and a breaking change (`!` or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer) → MAJOR. Other types are valid but release-neutral unless a tool is configured otherwise.

stem: An organization wants a support engineer to label, assign and close issues and pull requests, but never push code. Which repository role fits best?

options.text: Read
options.why: Read can open and comment on issues but can't manage labels or close others' issues.

options.text: Triage
options.why: Triage is for managing issues and PRs without write access to code.

options.text: Write
options.why: Write grants push access, which the engineer must not have.

options.text: Maintain
options.why: Maintain includes push and repository management, far more than needed.

explanation: Least privilege: Triage lets someone apply labels, assign people, and close or reopen issues and pull requests, without push access. Write, Maintain and Admin all include pushing code.
reference: GitHub docs: Repository roles for an organization

stem: Put the steps of GitHub Flow in order for a single change.

options.text: Create a branch from `main`
options.why: Work starts on a short-lived branch.

options.text: Commit changes and push the branch
options.why: Commits are shared by pushing the branch.

options.text: Open a pull request and get review and CI feedback
options.why: The PR is where discussion and checks happen.

options.text: Merge the pull request into `main`
options.why: Merging happens after approval and green checks.

options.text: Deploy and delete the branch
options.why: main is deployable; the merged branch is cleaned up.

explanation: Branch → commit and push → open a PR → review and checks → merge → deploy and delete the branch. Some teams deploy the branch before merging, but main stays the single source of releasable code.

stem: A PR targeting `develop` says `Closes #48` in its description. It is merged into `develop`, but issue #48 stays open. Why?

options.text: `Closes` is not a valid closing keyword; only `Fixes` works
options.why: `close`, `closes` and `closed` are all valid closing keywords.

options.text: Closing keywords only work for PRs that target the default branch
options.why: The PR targets `develop`, which isn't the default branch, so the keyword is ignored.

options.text: Issues only close when someone with Admin access merges the PR
options.why: Any merge into the default branch with a keyword closes the issue.

options.text: The keyword must appear in a commit message, not the PR description
options.why: Keywords work in PR descriptions; commit messages are an alternative.

explanation: GitHub interprets closing keywords in a PR description only when the PR targets the default branch. With GitFlow, issues therefore close when the release reaches `main`, or the team closes them by hand. Making `develop` the default branch is another fix.
reference: GitHub docs: Linking a pull request to an issue

stem: With the branch protection setting "Require linear history" enabled, pull requests can still be merged with "Squash and merge" or "Rebase and merge".

options.text: True
options.why: The setting only forbids merge commits; squash and rebase merges stay allowed.

options.text: False
options.why: Linear history rules out merge commits only, and both other methods produce linear history.

explanation: "Require linear history" prevents merge commits from being pushed to the branch, so PRs must be merged with squash or rebase. Make sure at least one of those methods is enabled in the repository settings.

stem: Which practices make a pull request easier to review? (Choose two.)

options.text: Keep it focused on one change and reasonably small
options.why: Small, single-purpose PRs are reviewed faster and more thoroughly.

options.text: Explain the why and how to test it, and link the issue
options.why: Context lets reviewers judge the approach, not just the diff.

options.text: Bundle the refactor, the feature and a formatting pass together
options.why: Mixed changes hide the real diff and slow the review.

options.text: Leave the description empty so the code speaks for itself
options.why: Reviewers then have to reverse-engineer intent from the diff.

options.text: Request review from the whole organization to get it seen quickly
options.why: Broad requests diffuse responsibility; ask the right owners.

explanation: Good PRs are small, focused and self-explanatory: what changed, why, how to verify it, and which issue it addresses. Separate mechanical changes such as formatting into their own PR.
reference: GitHub docs: Helping others review your changes

stem: A maintainer types the same "Thanks! Please add a test that reproduces the bug" comment on many PRs. Which GitHub feature is designed for this?

options.text: Saved replies
options.why: Saved replies store reusable comment text you can insert from the comment box.

options.text: Issue forms
options.why: Issue forms structure new issues; they don't insert comments.

options.text: CODEOWNERS
options.why: CODEOWNERS routes review requests; it doesn't write comments.

options.text: Pull request templates
options.why: Templates prefill the PR description written by the author, not maintainer replies.

explanation: Saved replies are personal canned responses available in issue and PR comment boxes. They keep common answers consistent and save typing.

stem: A README links to `docs/setup.md`. Readers browsing the `release-2` branch on GitHub click the link. Which link style keeps them on `release-2`?

options.text: `https://github.com/acme/app/blob/main/docs/setup.md`
options.why: An absolute link to `main` always jumps to main, whatever branch you browse.

options.text: `[Setup](docs/setup.md)`
options.why: Relative links resolve against the branch being viewed.

options.text: `[Setup](/blob/HEAD/docs/setup.md)`
options.why: This isn't a valid repository-relative path and doesn't follow the viewed branch.

options.text: `[Setup](setup)`
options.why: It points to a non-existent file, so the link breaks on every branch.

explanation: GitHub resolves relative links in Markdown files against the current branch, so they keep working on forks and other branches. Hard-coded absolute URLs pin readers to one branch.

stem: A team uses GitFlow. A critical bug is found in production (`main`) while `develop` holds unreleased features. What is the GitFlow way to ship the fix?

options.text: Fix it on `develop` and release everything currently on `develop`
options.why: That ships unfinished features along with the fix.

options.text: Branch `hotfix/*` from `main`, then merge it into both `main` and `develop`
options.why: Hotfixes start from production and are merged back so `develop` keeps the fix.

options.text: Commit the fix straight to `main` and skip `develop`
options.why: `develop` would later reintroduce the bug at the next release.

options.text: Create a feature branch from `develop` and fast-track it straight into the next release
options.why: Features branch from develop and wait for a release; they don't patch production.

explanation: In GitFlow, hotfix branches come off `main` (the released code), get tagged when merged into `main`, and are also merged into `develop` (or into the open release branch). Skipping the merge back is how fixed bugs come back.
reference: Driessen: A successful Git branching model

stem: A PR branch already sits directly on top of the latest `main`. It is merged with GitHub's "Rebase and merge". How do the commits on `main` compare with those on the PR branch?

options.text: Same SHAs, because the branch was already up to date and nothing needed replaying
options.why: That is how a local fast-forward behaves, not GitHub's rebase and merge.

options.text: New SHAs, because GitHub always rewrites the committer data
options.why: Rebase and merge on GitHub always updates committer info and creates new SHAs.

options.text: One squashed commit containing all of the PR's changes
options.why: Squashing is a different merge method; rebase keeps each commit.

options.text: The original commits plus a two-parent merge commit on top
options.why: Rebase and merge never creates a merge commit.

explanation: GitHub documents that rebase and merge always updates the committer information and creates new SHAs, even when the branch is already up to date, unlike `git rebase` locally. Local branches still pointing at the old commits will look unmerged.
reference: GitHub docs: About pull request merges

stem: Branch protection on `main` requires 1 approval and has "Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed" enabled. After Bob approves, the author pushes a one-line typo fix. What is the PR's state?

options.text: Still approved, because the change is tiny
options.why: GitHub doesn't judge size; any change to the diff makes the approval stale.

options.text: Bob's approval is dismissed and a new approval is needed
options.why: The approved diff changed, so the approval is dismissed as stale.

options.text: Still approved, but the PR becomes a draft until Bob re-reviews
options.why: Stale approvals don't convert a PR to a draft.

options.text: Blocked until an admin overrides branch protection
options.why: Any eligible reviewer can approve again; no admin is required.

explanation: GitHub records the diff a reviewer approved. If it changes (new commits, Update branch, or a related merge into the base), the approval is dismissed as stale and someone must approve again.

stem: A team wants every change on `main` to be reviewed, to pass CI, and to arrive without merge commits. Which branch protection settings achieve this? (Choose three.)

options.text: Require a pull request with at least one approving review
options.why: This forces review before merging.

options.text: Require status checks to pass before merging
options.why: This gates merging on CI results.

options.text: Require linear history
options.why: This rejects merge commits, so squash or rebase merges are used.

options.text: Allow force pushes for everyone
options.why: Force pushes let people rewrite or bypass reviewed history.

options.text: Allow deletions of the protected branch
options.why: Deleting `main` has nothing to do with review, CI or history shape.

options.text: Lock branch
options.why: Locking makes the branch read-only, which stops all merges.

explanation: Required reviews, required status checks and required linear history together cover review, testing and history shape. Force pushes and deletions are disabled by default on protected branches and should stay that way.

stem: A library is at version `1.4.2` and follows Conventional Commits with SemVer. Since that release the commits are `fix: correct rounding` and `feat: add CSV export`. What is the next version? Type it as `x.y.z`.
explanation: The highest-ranked change wins: a `feat` means MINOR, which outranks the `fix` PATCH. A minor bump resets the patch number, so 1.4.2 becomes 1.5.0, not 1.5.2.

stem: A developer squash-merged `feature/search` into `main`, then kept committing on the same branch and opened a second PR. Why does the second PR show the already-merged work again and conflict more often?

options.text: Squash merges delete the head branch, so the second PR has to start again completely from scratch
options.why: The branch can be kept; the issue is ancestry, not deletion.

options.text: The squash commit is new, so the branch's old commits never became ancestors of `main`
options.why: Git can't see that those commits were merged, so they reappear in the comparison.

options.text: GitHub blocks a second PR from a branch that was already merged once
options.why: GitHub allows it; the history is just messier.

options.text: Squash merges rewrite the commits on the feature branch itself
options.why: Squashing creates a new commit on the base; the head branch is unchanged.

explanation: Squash and merge works best for short-lived branches. Because the squash commit is unrelated to the branch's commits, later PRs from that branch include the already-squashed commits and can force you to resolve the same conflicts again. Start a fresh branch from main, rebase, or use merge commits for long-running branches.
reference: GitHub docs: About pull request merges (squashing a long-running branch)

stem: A developer opens a draft PR that changes files owned by `@acme/payments` in CODEOWNERS. When is the payments team automatically requested for review?

options.text: Immediately when the draft is opened
options.why: Code owners are deliberately not requested on draft PRs.

options.text: When the PR is marked ready for review
options.why: Marking a draft ready notifies the code owners and requests their review.

options.text: Only after all required status checks have passed
options.why: Review requests aren't tied to status checks.

options.text: Never; code owners must always be requested by hand
options.why: Automatic requests are the main purpose of CODEOWNERS.

explanation: Code owners aren't automatically requested to review draft pull requests. Once the PR is marked ready for review, they are notified. This keeps owners from being pinged about unfinished work.

stem: Match each GitHub merge method with its effect on `main`.

options.text: Create a merge commit
options.why: Keeps the PR commits and adds a commit with two parents.

options.text: Squash and merge
options.why: Adds one new commit containing the whole PR.

options.text: Rebase and merge
options.why: Replays each PR commit individually with new SHAs.

prompts.text: Every commit from the PR keeps its original SHA, and the branch topology stays visible
History stays linear and each PR appears as exactly one commit
History stays linear but each PR commit appears separately

explanation: A merge commit preserves the original commits and records the merge. Squash collapses the PR into one commit. Rebase and merge keeps individual commits but rewrites them onto the base, producing new SHAs and no merge commit.
reference: GitHub docs: About merge methods on GitHub

stem: `main` requires status checks and "Require branches to be up to date before merging". With 20 PRs ready each day, authors keep clicking Update branch and rerunning CI, only to be beaten by another merge. Which GitHub feature addresses this?

options.text: Turn off required status checks for busy days
options.why: That trades the pile-up for untested code on main.

options.text: A merge queue
options.why: The queue tests each PR against the base plus the PRs ahead of it, then merges in order.

options.text: Allow force pushes to `main` for maintainers
options.why: Force pushes don't help ordering and risk rewriting history.

options.text: Convert every PR to a draft until its turn comes
options.why: Drafts can't merge, and nothing would test them against the latest base.

explanation: A merge queue automates the "update, retest, merge" loop: queued PRs are tested together with the changes ahead of them, and are merged only if the combination passes. Busy branches keep their CI guarantees without manual rebasing.
reference: GitHub docs: Managing a merge queue

stem: A SaaS team deploys to production many times a day and wants to avoid long-lived branches and big merge conflicts. Which model fits best?

options.text: Trunk-based development with short-lived branches and feature flags
options.why: Small changes merge to trunk quickly, and flags hide unfinished work.

options.text: GitFlow with scheduled release branches
options.why: GitFlow suits versioned, scheduled releases, not continuous deployment.

options.text: One long-lived branch per developer, merged monthly
options.why: Long-lived branches cause exactly the big conflicts the team wants to avoid.

options.text: Release branches cut before every single deploy
options.why: Cutting a branch per deploy adds ceremony with no benefit at this pace.

explanation: Trunk-based development keeps everyone integrating into one branch at least daily, relying on CI and feature flags to keep trunk releasable. It pairs naturally with continuous delivery; GitFlow fits products with explicit versioned releases.

stem: In GitFlow, put the steps of shipping version 2.3.0 in order.

options.text: Create `release/2.3.0` from `develop`
options.why: Release prep starts from the integration branch.

options.text: Fix release bugs and bump the version on the release branch
options.why: Only stabilisation work happens here.

options.text: Merge the release branch into `main` and tag `v2.3.0`
options.why: main receives the finished release and its tag.

options.text: Merge the release branch back into `develop`
options.why: This keeps the release fixes in ongoing work.

options.text: Delete the release branch
options.why: Clean up once both merges are done.

explanation: A release branch is cut from `develop`, stabilised, merged into `main` and tagged, then merged back into `develop` so fixes aren't lost, and finally deleted. New features keep flowing into `develop` meanwhile.
reference: Driessen: A successful Git branching model

stem: A PR into the default branch should close both #34 and #35 when merged. Which descriptions do that? (Choose two.)

options.text: `Fixes #34, fixes #35`
options.why: Each issue reference has its own closing keyword.

options.text: `Resolves #34` on one line and `Closes #35` on another
options.why: Different valid keywords can be mixed, one per issue.
The keyword applies only to the first reference; #35 is just linked.

options.text: `Fixes #34 and #35 (both related)`
options.why: Again only #34 has a keyword in front of it.

options.text: `Related: #34 #35`
options.why: "Related" is not a closing keyword, so neither issue closes.

explanation: To close several issues, repeat a closing keyword before every reference, for example `Resolves #10, resolves #123`. A shared keyword applies only to the reference right after it.
reference: GitHub docs: Linking a pull request to an issue

stem: If two GitHub rulesets target the same branch and define the same rule differently, the most restrictive version of that rule is enforced.

options.text: True
options.why: Rulesets have no priority; rules are aggregated and the strictest version applies.

options.text: False
options.why: GitHub documents that layered rulesets aggregate, with the most restrictive version of a rule winning.

explanation: Unlike branch protection rules, where one rule applies per branch, several rulesets can apply at once. Their rules are combined, and conflicting settings resolve to the most restrictive one. Rulesets also layer with any branch protection rules on the same branch.

stem: Which statements about `Co-authored-by` commit trailers are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: They go at the end of the message, after a blank line, as `Co-authored-by: Name <email>`
options.why: Trailers live in the final paragraph of the message.

options.text: GitHub attributes the commit to each listed co-author whose email matches their account
options.why: Co-authors appear on the commit and in their contribution graphs.

options.text: They change the commit's author field to list several people
options.why: Git still records one author; co-authors exist only as trailers.

options.text: They only work when added through the GitHub web editor
options.why: Any Git client can write them; they are plain text in the message.

options.text: They can be placed anywhere in the subject line
options.why: In the subject they are ordinary text and GitHub ignores them.

explanation: Add one `Co-authored-by: Name <email@example.com>` line per co-author at the end of the commit message, after a blank line. The email must be associated with the co-author's GitHub account (a noreply address works) for attribution.
reference: GitHub docs: Creating a commit with multiple authors

stem: `main` requires one approving review. Carol (Write access) submits "Request changes" on a PR, and then Dave approves it. Can the PR be merged?

options.text: Yes, because Dave's approval meets the one-approval requirement
options.why: An outstanding change request still blocks merging.

options.text: No, not until Carol approves or her review is dismissed
options.why: A change request from a writer blocks merging until it is resolved.

options.text: Yes, because the most recent review always wins
options.why: Reviews from different people don't override each other.

options.text: No, because a second approval from an Admin is now required
options.why: There's no extra admin requirement; the change request must be cleared.

explanation: With required reviews enabled, a "Request changes" review from someone with write or admin access blocks merging. It stays blocking until that reviewer approves, or someone allowed to dismiss reviews dismisses it.

stem: A project at version `1.4.2` uses Conventional Commits with SemVer. The only commit since the last release is `feat!: drop support for Node 18`. What is the next version? Type it as `x.y.z`.
explanation: The `!` after the type marks a breaking change, which means a MAJOR bump regardless of the type. A major bump resets minor and patch, so 1.4.2 becomes 2.0.0.

stem: A PR shows "Expected — Waiting for status to be reported" for the required check `ci / test`, so it can never be merged. What are likely causes? (Choose two.)

options.text: The job was renamed, so no check named `ci / test` reports anymore
options.why: Branch protection matches checks by exact name.

options.text: The workflow was skipped by a path filter, so the required check never ran
options.why: A required check that never reports stays pending forever.

options.text: The PR has too many commits for status checks to report
options.why: There is no commit-count limit on reporting checks.

options.text: Required checks only run after an approving review is submitted
options.why: Checks run on push or PR events, independently of reviews.

options.text: The author lacks Write access, so checks are hidden from them
options.why: Visibility of results doesn't stop a check from reporting.

explanation: Required status checks are matched by name. If no check with that name reports for the head commit (renamed job, deleted workflow, or a workflow skipped by path or branch filters), the requirement stays pending and blocks merging. Fix the name or make sure the check always reports.
reference: GitHub docs: Troubleshooting required status checks

stem: CODEOWNERS assigns `/infra/ @acme/sre`, but nobody is requested for review on PRs touching `infra/`. The team is visible. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Team owners must be listed by email, not as `@org/team`
options.why: Teams are written as `@org/team-name`; emails are for users.

options.text: The `sre` team doesn't have write access to the repository
options.why: Code owners, including teams, need write permission to be requested.

options.text: CODEOWNERS only works in the repository root, not in `.github/`
options.why: `.github/`, the root and `docs/` are all supported locations.

options.text: Directory patterns need a trailing `/**` to match nested files
options.why: `/infra/` already matches everything under that directory.

explanation: People and teams listed as code owners must have write permissions, and a team must be visible and have write access itself, even if every member individually does. Otherwise GitHub silently skips the request.

stem: Branch protection requires one approval with "Require approval of the most recent reviewable push", without dismissing stale approvals. Erin approves, then Erin herself pushes a fix to the PR branch. What is needed to merge?

options.text: Nothing; Erin's earlier approval still counts
options.why: The most recent push must be approved by someone other than the pusher.

options.text: An approval from someone other than Erin, who made the latest push
options.why: This rule stops the last pusher from approving their own unreviewed change.

options.text: Erin re-approving her own push
options.why: The person who made the last push can't satisfy the requirement.

options.text: An admin bypass, because approvals are now locked
options.why: Any other eligible reviewer can approve; no bypass is needed.

explanation: This option protects against someone pushing unreviewed code after an approval. Earlier approvals aren't dismissed, but the most recent push must be approved by someone other than the person who made it.

stem: Match each situation with the branching approach that fits it best.

options.text: Trunk-based development
options.why: Integrate into one branch continuously, behind feature flags.

options.text: GitFlow
options.why: develop, release and hotfix branches for scheduled releases.

options.text: Release branches kept for maintenance
options.why: Long-lived branches per supported version receiving backported fixes.

prompts.text: A web app deployed many times a day from a single branch
A desktop app shipping a planned version every quarter, with hotfixes in between
A database driver that must patch versions 3.x and 4.x for years

explanation: Continuous deployment favours trunk-based development. Scheduled, versioned releases map well onto GitFlow. Supporting several released versions at once needs maintenance branches (such as `release/3.x`) that receive cherry-picked fixes.

stem: A GitFlow team cuts `release/2.3`, fixes three bugs on it, merges it into `main` and tags `v2.3.0`, but forgets to merge it back into `develop`. What happens at the next release?

options.text: Nothing, because Git copies tagged commits into every branch
options.why: Tags are pointers; they don't propagate commits anywhere.

options.text: Release 2.4 is cut from `develop`, which lacks the fixes, so the bugs come back
options.why: The fixes exist only on the release branch and main.

options.text: The 2.4 merge into `main` fails until someone merges the tag
options.why: The merge succeeds; the problem is the missing fixes, not a failure.

options.text: GitHub auto-syncs `develop` with `main` after every tag
options.why: GitHub has no such automatic sync.

explanation: Release and hotfix branches must be merged back into `develop`. Otherwise the next release, cut from `develop`, ships without those fixes. Teams often add a checklist item or automation to enforce the back-merge.
reference: Driessen: A successful Git branching model

stem: Put the steps of a PR going through a GitHub merge queue in order.

options.text: The PR is approved and its required checks pass
options.why: Only mergeable PRs can join the queue.

options.text: The author adds the PR to the merge queue
options.why: Adding to the queue replaces clicking Merge.

options.text: GitHub builds a temporary branch with the base, PRs ahead in the queue, and this PR
options.why: This tests the PR against what main will actually be.

options.text: Required checks run on that temporary branch
options.why: CI validates the combined changes.

options.text: If they pass, the PR is merged into the base in queue order
options.why: Failures remove the PR from the queue instead.

explanation: A merge queue makes each PR prove it works on top of the latest base plus everything ahead of it. CI must be configured to run for merge-queue events, otherwise required checks never report for the temporary branch.
reference: GitHub docs: Managing a merge queue

stem: You are asked to review a 3,000-line PR that mixes a refactor and a new feature. Which responses are most effective? (Choose three.)

options.text: Ask the author to split it into smaller, separately reviewable PRs
options.why: Smaller PRs get real review instead of skimming.

options.text: Review the overall design and approach before line-level details
options.why: Catching a wrong approach early saves the most rework.

options.text: Review commit by commit if the history separates the refactor from the feature
options.why: Well-structured commits make large diffs digestible.

options.text: Approve quickly, since CI passed and the change is large anyway
options.why: Green CI isn't a substitute for review, especially for big changes.

options.text: Comment on every style nit first so nothing is missed
options.why: Nit-picking up front buries the important feedback.

options.text: Rewrite the feature yourself on a new branch
options.why: That bypasses the author and the collaborative review process.

explanation: For oversized PRs, push for smaller ones, review design first, and use commits or file groups to break the work down. Leave automatable style issues to linters and mark optional nits as such.

stem:
A project follows Conventional Commits with SemVer and is at `3.2.1`. The only new commit is:

```
docs: rewrite configuration guide

BREAKING CHANGE: the `timeout` option is now in seconds, not milliseconds
```

What is the next version?

options.text: No release, because `docs` commits never trigger one
options.why: A `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer makes any commit type breaking.

options.text: `3.2.2`, because docs changes count as a patch
options.why: The footer signals a breaking change, which outranks a patch.

options.text: `4.0.0`, because the footer marks a breaking change
options.why: A breaking change means MAJOR, whatever the type prefix says.

options.text: `3.3.0`, because the footer upgrades the commit to a feature
options.why: Breaking changes map to MAJOR, not MINOR.

explanation: In Conventional Commits, a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer (or `!` after the type) marks a breaking change in a commit of any type and maps to a MAJOR version. The commit was also mis-typed: changing an option's unit isn't a docs-only change.

stem: Several teammates have checked out a long-running shared PR branch. It conflicts with `main`. Which way of updating it avoids disrupting them?

options.text: Rebase the branch onto `main` and force-push
options.why: Rewriting a shared branch forces everyone to recover their local copies.

options.text: Merge `main` into the PR branch, resolve conflicts and push normally
options.why: A merge only adds a commit, so teammates can pull without rewriting history.

options.text: Use "Update branch" with the rebase option
options.why: That also rewrites the shared branch's history.

options.text: Close the PR and open a fresh one from `main`
options.why: Throwing away the branch loses work and review context.

explanation: Rebasing rewrites commits, which is fine for a private branch but painful for shared ones. Merging the base into the head branch (the default "Update branch") adds a merge commit and keeps everyone's clones valid. Squash merging the PR later still keeps `main` tidy.
reference: GitHub docs: Keeping your pull request in sync with the base branch

stem: Which are genuine advantages of GitHub rulesets over classic branch protection rules? (Choose two.)

options.text: Several rulesets can apply to the same branch at once
options.why: Only one branch protection rule applies per branch.

options.text: A ruleset can be disabled without deleting it
options.why: Enforcement status can be switched off and on again.

options.text: Rulesets are applied in a priority order you choose
options.why: Rulesets have no priority; their rules are aggregated.

options.text: Rulesets let admins bypass rules silently with no configuration
options.why: Bypass must be granted explicitly through a bypass list.

options.text: Rulesets replace and switch off any branch protection rules
options.why: Rulesets layer with branch protection rules; both are enforced.

explanation: Rulesets can stack (rules are aggregated, most restrictive wins), have enforcement statuses so you can disable them without deleting, and are visible to anyone with read access. They work alongside existing branch protection rules rather than replacing them.
